extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent applicants, and courts (patent bar, PTO/PTAB practitioners, appellate counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of whether pure AIA (post‑March 16, 2013) patents can be included in interference proceedings, explaining AIA § 3(n)’s effective‑date rules, the pre‑AIA interference provisions, and related statutory‑interpretation principles and remedies under the AIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA first‑inventor‑to‑file rule (post‑AIA patentability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the AIA, the first person to file a patent application on an invention has priority and is entitled to a patent, even when another inventor can establish an earlier invention date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AIA changed prior art and obviousness to be evaluated from the 'effective filing date' of the claimed invention; Congress enacted this to provide objectivity and certainty and to harmonize with other countries. See AIA § 3(b)–(c); AIA § 3(o),(p).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑AIA first‑to‑invent rule (pre‑AIA patentability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under pre‑AIA law the first person to invent a claimed invention had priority and was entitled to a patent, even if another inventor first filed a patent application; pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(g) and interference proceedings determined priority of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference proceedings were lengthy, costly, and required corroborating evidence of invention date; were a central reason Congress moved to first‑inventor‑to‑file. See pre‑AIA §§ 102(g), 135; H.R. Rep. No. 112‑98.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement of interferences by derivation proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA repealed interference provisions and replaced them with derivation proceedings to address situations where an earlier filer may have derived the claimed invention from a later filer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AIA §§ 3(h)–(i) (amending 35 U.S.C. §§ 135, 291); interferences determined first inventor; derivation determines whether earlier filer derived the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA § 3(n)(1) effective‑date rule (when AIA amendments 'shall apply')
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA's amendments 'shall apply' to any application or patent that contains or contained at any time a claim with an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'shall' is mandatory; therefore patents/claims with effective filing dates on/after March 16, 2013 are governed by the AIA (first‑inventor‑to‑file) and not by pre‑AIA invention‑priority rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA § 3(n)(2) mixed‑patent exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application or patent that is otherwise subject to the AIA also contains or contained at any time a claim with an effective filing date before March 16, 2013, then the pre‑AIA Interference Provisions (sections 102(g), 135, 291 as of March 15, 2013) shall apply to each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a limited class ('mixed patents/applications') that remain subject to interferences despite containing AIA‑governed claims; Congress explicitly enumerated this exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three AIA § 3(n) patent categories and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA § 3(n) creates: (1) Pure pre‑AIA patents/applications (only pre‑AIA effective filing dates) subject to pre‑AIA patentability and interferences; (2) Pure AIA patents/applications (only post‑March 16, 2013 effective filing dates) subject to AIA patentability and derivations; (3) Mixed patents/applications (contain both pre‑ and post‑effective filing date claims) subject to AIA patentability but also to pre‑AIA interference provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying which category a patent/application falls into determines whether interferences or derivations and which statutory standards apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'any unexpired patent' in pre‑AIA § 135 (contextual limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'any unexpired patent' in pre‑AIA § 135, when read in context with AIA § 3(n), does not include pure AIA patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read statutes together: AIA § 3(n) specifically circumscribes which patents are subject to interferences; interpreting 'any unexpired patent' to reach pure AIA patents would be inconsistent with AIA § 3(n) and the AIA’s repeal of interferences for AIA patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory‑interpretation starting point: plain text, context, structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory interpretation begins with the statutory language; plain meaning is derived from text and structure, read in context of the overall statutory scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cases like McEntee and King: read words in context, with regard to purpose and statutory structure; do not construe isolated provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific statute controls over general statute
rubrics_metrics.description: When a specific statutory provision addresses a situation, it controls over a more general provision even without regard to enactment priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Bulova Watch Co. principle: AIA § 3(n) (specific effective‑date rules) controls over the more general 'any unexpired patent' language in pre‑AIA § 135.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon against surplusage (avoid rendering provisions superfluous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretations that would render another part of the same statutory scheme superfluous should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because AIA § 3(n)(2) specifically creates the mixed‑patent exception, interpreting pre‑AIA § 135 to already reach pure AIA patents would make § 3(n)(2) superfluous; apply Bilski/Marx guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative purpose informs interpretation: elimination of interferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress enacted the AIA in part to eliminate interference proceedings as lengthy, costly, and burdensome and to provide certainty by using filing dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use legislative history (H.R. Rep. No. 112‑98, S. Rep. No. 111‑18) to support a reading that does not expose pure AIA patents to interferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for statutory interpretation in appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory interpretation by the court is a question of law reviewed de novo on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply de novo review (VirnetX v. Apple cited); Patent Office did not claim Chevron deference here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available post‑grant/patent‑reexamination mechanisms under the AIA
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter partes review (IPR), post‑grant review (PGR), and ex parte reexamination are mechanisms to challenge or reconsider issued patents under the AIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mechanisms can address overlapping grants instead of using interferences to resolve priority between pre‑AIA applications and pure AIA patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA prior‑art and obviousness timing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the AIA prior art is measured relative to the 'effective filing date' of the claimed invention, and obviousness is considered from the effective filing date (35 U.S.C. § 102; 35 U.S.C. § 103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with pre‑AIA where prior art and obviousness were evaluated with respect to the date of invention; the AIA's change underpins why interferences are unnecessary for AIA patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accorded benefit date and senior/junior party determination in interferences
rubrics_metrics.description: In impairment/ interference practice the Board accords benefit dates to parties (e.g., senior: earlier‑filed application/benefit date; junior: later‑filed) and uses those benefit dates to assign senior/junior status and determine whether priority has been overcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefit dates reflect constructive reduction to practice for pre‑AIA § 102(g) analyses; absence of a priority statement asserting an earlier invention date can result in judgment against the junior party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion/controlling rule from this decision: pure AIA patents may not be part of an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure AIA patents—those with effective filing dates on or after March 16, 2013 and that have only ever contained post‑AIA effective filing date claims—are not subject to interference proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the AIA's amendments 'shall apply' to such patents and AIA § 3(n) creates a limited exception only for mixed patents, the Director erred in declaring an interference involving pure AIA patents; the court reversed.
